passage:
'Your phone's ringing,' Ira said from the doorway of their shared room. Aadhya's big sister never knocked.
'Let it.' Aadhya didn't look up from the bed. 'It's Kritika. She'll want to talk.'
'Isn't that the point of a phone?'
'She'll ask about Saturday. I'm not going to the mall.'
'You love the mall. And you skipped the birthday lunch last week.'
'Because everyone would be there. And the class group keeps pinging about the project, so I muted it.'
Ira sat on the edge of the bed. 'Since when?'
'Since the presentation. I got out of that and it was such a relief. Now everything feels like a presentation.' Aadhya pulled the pillow over her face. 'Don't look at me like that.'
'Like what?'
'Like you're worried. I'm fine. I just don't want to do anything.'
The phone stopped ringing. The silence felt worse.

qa.q: Who was calling Aadhya?
qa.a: Kritika was calling.

qa.q: What does Aadhya mean when she says 'Now everything feels like a presentation'?
qa.a: She means that after the relief of escaping the presentation, ordinary things like calls, the mall and the group chat now feel just as threatening.

qa.q: What turning point could Ira help open at this stage?
qa.a: Ira could suggest one small step, like calling Kritika back together or going to the mall for an hour, and suggest talking to a school counsellor if the avoiding keeps growing.

qa.q: What is Ira experiencing as the phone stops ringing?
qa.a: Ira is worried, watching a sister who loved the mall shut friends out one by one, and is stung at being told not to look concerned.

grounding: It shows a teenager who escaped one presentation now dodging calls, outings and the group chat as her safe world shrinks.

passage:
It started with one debate round in September. I told Ma'am I had a sore throat, and the relief was so huge I nearly laughed.
By October I was letting calls go to voicemail. Not just unknown numbers, everyone. Dolma rang three times about the tuition carpool, and I texted 'got a lift' when I hadn't. I walked the forty minutes instead so I wouldn't have to talk in the car.
Then Sunday football went. Then the group chat. Each thing I dropped felt like one less danger, but the things left felt scarier. Even buying bread at the corner shop made my chest tight.
Looking back, Sahil in September would never have believed Sahil in November: a person whose safe world was basically a bedroom and a school desk.

qa.q: What excuse did Sahil give to skip the debate round?
qa.a: Sahil told Ma'am about having a sore throat.

qa.q: How did Sahil feel each time another activity was dropped?
qa.a: Each drop brought a short sense of safety, but what remained felt scarier, until even buying bread made Sahil's chest tight.

qa.q: What could have been a turning point for Sahil around October?
qa.a: Telling a parent or the school counsellor about the tight chest and the dodged calls could have led to small, supported steps back, like one carpool ride with Dolma.

qa.q: What might Dolma have been experiencing as the carpool offers kept being turned down?
qa.a: Dolma might have felt puzzled or brushed off after three calls and a 'got a lift' text, not knowing Sahil was walking forty minutes to avoid talking.

grounding: It shows avoidance spreading from one debate round to calls, carpools, football and the group chat until the safe world shrinks to a bedroom and a desk.

passage:
After Tushar froze during the district debate in Sehore, with the whole school watching, he told himself he'd simply skip debates from now on.
But the avoiding spread. He stopped answering the landline, in case a relative asked about the debate. He stopped going to the vegetable market for his mother, because people there knew him. When his friends shouted from the lane for cricket, he pretended to be asleep. Last week he even let the tuition teacher's call ring out.
Each time he felt relief, like a door closing on a cold wind. And each time the next thing seemed a little scarier.
Parveen didi from next door found him on the roof on Sunday. "You used to be everywhere in this mohalla," she said. "Now I only see you up here."
Tushar shrugged. The world below looked noisy and sharp, and the roof felt like the only safe place left.

qa.q: Where did Tushar freeze?
qa.a: During the district debate in Sehore.

qa.q: What does Tushar's relief each time he avoids something show?
qa.a: He feels anxious, and the relief makes avoiding feel safe, so the fear spreads to more and more things.

qa.q: What could help Tushar at this stage?
qa.a: Starting with small steps back, like one market errand with his mother, and telling a trusted adult how scared he feels.

qa.q: How does Parveen didi see the change in Tushar?
qa.a: She is surprised and concerned, missing the boy who used to be everywhere in the mohalla.

grounding: After freezing at a debate, a teen avoids the phone, errands and friends, and each relief makes the world feel more threatening.

passage:
After Mei's voice cracked during her class presentation in Singapore, she decided she would just stay quiet in class for a while.
But the quiet grew. She muted the class group chat. She stopped going to the hawker centre after school with the others, in case Tariq brought up the presentation. When her phone rang, even with her aunt's name on the screen, her chest tightened and she let it go to voicemail. On Saturday she skipped the badminton club she had loved since primary school.
Each time she felt a quick flood of relief. Then, a little later, the next thing felt harder.
Tariq caught her at the lockers on Monday. "Hey, the group project's on Thursday. You'll come?"
Mei's heart raced. "Maybe. I'll see."
She knew she wouldn't. Her world was getting smaller, and everything outside it felt sharper every week.

qa.q: What club did Mei skip on Saturday?
qa.a: The badminton club she had loved since primary school.

qa.q: What does Mei's racing heart at Tariq's question show?
qa.a: She feels anxious and trapped, as even a simple invitation now feels threatening.

qa.q: What could Mei try before Thursday?
qa.a: Tell Tariq or a trusted adult honestly about the fear, and go to the group project for at least part of the time.

qa.q: What might Tariq notice about Mei?
qa.a: Tariq may notice her pulling away and feel puzzled or worried, not knowing it started with the presentation.

grounding: After one shaky presentation a teen avoids chats, outings, calls and her club, and her circle of safe activities keeps shrinking.

passage: At the school canteen, Gopika put her tray down across from Siddharth. "You didn't reply in the group. We're going bowling on Saturday." Siddharth shrugged. "Didn't see it." He had seen it; he had muted the chat a week ago. It had started with the history presentation last month. He'd faked a cough and skipped it, and the relief had been huge. Then the group chat felt risky too, all those people who might mention it. Then Saturday outings. Now, when his phone rang, even when it was his uncle, his stomach clenched and he let it ring out. "You've been weird," Gopika said. "Everyone thinks you're angry with us." "I'm not." He meant it. He just wanted them to stop asking. Walking back to class, he took the long way to avoid the corridor where the history teacher sat.

qa.q: What did Siddharth fake to skip the history presentation?
qa.a: He faked a cough and skipped it.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling when his phone rang?
qa.a: Siddharth felt anxious, with his stomach clenching, even when it was only his uncle, so he let it ring out.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Siddharth at this stage?
qa.a: He could tell Gopika honestly that he has been anxious, try one small step like replying in the group, and talk to a trusted adult or the school counsellor about the fear.

qa.q: How might Gopika see Siddharth's silence?
qa.a: Gopika and the others read it as anger with them, which leaves Gopika hurt and confused when it is really fear.

grounding: Shows a teenager who avoided one presentation now dodging chats, outings and calls, his safe world shrinking.
